newsitem.title: USA: Montgomery Ward says recruiting by Sears halted.
newsitem.headline: Montgomery Ward says recruiting by Sears halted.

text.p: A U.S. bankruptcy court granted Montgomery Ward Holding Co. a temporary restraining order blocking rival Sears, Roebuck and Co. from recruiting employees from the ailing retailer's management ranks, Montgomery Ward said Tuesday.
The order, which prohibits Sears from approaching, contacting or soliciting for employment any current management employee of Montgomery Ward, was granted Monday by a bankruptcy court in Delaware.
The order stemmed from a motion by Montgomery Ward alleging predatory recruiting practices by Sears.

The motion alleged Sears had engaged in conduct designed to "hasten the weakening state of Montgomery Ward" and "make it even more difficult for (Ward) to do business," Montgomery Ward said in a statement.

Chicago-based Montgomery Ward filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection last month after talks with lenders to restructure its debt and obtain new financing fell apart. The 125-year-old department store chain racked up losses worth $249 million in 1996.
Sears said its corporate policy discourages recruiting employees from struggling competitors.
"Despite the fact that we are in a competitive business, we have a crystal clear policy on matters such as this," said Sears spokesman Ron Culp.
"If this indeed happened, it was against these guidelines and we will take appropriate actions to see this doesn't happen again," he said, adding, "We will also reissue the policy today."

Culp said the policy sets forth guidelines for when a competitor is failing. In dealing with job applicants, "It lets them contact us," and cautions against being overly zealous or overly aggressive in pursuing employees at another company, he said.

Montgomery Ward alleged that a Sears "Action Plan" was distributed via electronic mail to Sears field locations and targeted specific key positions in recruiting efforts designed solely to hurt Montgomery Ward's business. It told Sears personnel to be "extremely predatory" in their methods, Ward said.

Montgomery Ward said Sears human resource representatives began systematically contacting Montgomery Ward personnel in targeted jobs, and recruiters were told to keep a headcount of how many people they could hire away.

"Obviously, our first priority is to fix our business and we believe that we can compete with any retailer in a fair business environment. However, based on this 'Action Plan' we believe that Sears has crossed the line between healthy competition and unethical activities," said Montgomery Ward Chairman Roger Goddu.

Montgomery Ward is the largest privately held retailer in the United States, currently operating a chain of 400 stores in 43 states. After a planned closing of its speciality stores, Montgomery Ward will operate 356 stores in 39 states.
